newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria's leaders begin disputed reforms conference.
newsitem.headline: Algeria's leaders begin disputed reforms conference.

text.p: Algeria's embattled leadership and about 1,000 politicians start a controversial conference on Saturday to chart reform plans to pull Algeria out of nearly five years of civil strife.

Algiers residents said the government had deployed heavy security on roads to and around the venue of the much-vaunted "National Conference of Understanding" at the seaside complex of Palais des Nations, 20 km (12 miles), from the capital.
The deployment underscored the continued killings in the North African gas and oil producing country, much of it hidden from the public through tight censorship of the media.
An estimated 50,000 people have been killed since January 1992 when the authorities scrapped a general election in which Moslem fundamentalist had taken a commanding lead.
Just two days ahead of the conference, a car bomb exploded in southern Algiers killing two people and wounding 28, said eyewitnesses and residents on Friday.
The booby-trapped car went off in the centre of Baraki, targeting a local security guard station, witnesses said by telephone from Algiers.
There was no official word about the bombing. No one claimed responsibility but the authorities have blamed Moslem guerrillas for bomb attacks over the past nearly five years.
The government-appointed rights watchdog, Human Rights National Observatory (ONDH), said in August that about 1,400 civilians had been killed by such bombs in the past two years.

Four legal opposition parties, including two main secular groups, are boycotting the conference, charging that it will be a rubber-stamp for reforms already decided largely by President Liamine Zeroual.
The authorities have also barred the once powerful Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), now outlawed, from the conference.

The FIS said earlier this week that leaders from 10 parties and social and union organisations taking part "would have to take entire responsibility for...the aggravation of the crisis with its accompanying destruction, misery and poverty".
Several Algerians interviewed by state-run television on Friday night said they hoped the conference would help bring peace and understanding among the country's politicians.

"We are longing for peace and an end to the bloodshed," said one young woman in her 20s. An old man condemned the violence: "It is enough. It is a must to secure peace and understanding for the sake of the young people."
Asked what he expected from the conference, a young man commented: "What we want is a normal life and a normal situation where anybody can get to work normally."
Political sources said they expected Zeroual to open the gathering with a speech in which he would underline his policy to establish a multiparty democracy through dialogue.
The television said the conference, convened after two years of tortuous talks, was expected to end on Sunday at noon by adopting a reforms platform.
This is expected to endorse Zeroual's main proposals:
-- A ban on the use of religion as a political weapon, although existing parties founded on religion, like the legal Hamas, will have a year to change their focus and conform;
-- Confirmation that Islam is the state religion of the country's 29 million people.
The two main secular opposition parties, the Socialist Forces Front (FFS) and the Rally for Democracy and Culture (RCD), are boycotting the conference.
Zeroual is also expected to confirm his plan to hold a referendum to amend the constitution in the next three months and hold general and local elections in 1997.
